index: Nicomaque

**Nicomaque** is a backgammon tournament engine. It is not an application you open: it is a library that other software uses to run a tournament — registering players, pairing matches, keeping the brackets, producing the standings.
It is written in Go, with no dependency at all, and can be read from end to end. It is released under a free licence and its code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/PileOfCells/backgammon-tournoi).
What it does
A tournament director spends the day answering a single question: *who plays whom, right now, and on which table?* Nicomaque answers that question, and nothing else.

At any moment it proposes a list of actions — start this match on that table, give this bye, draw this bracket, move to the next phase, close the tournament. The director confirms whichever he wants. Each confirmation becomes an **event** appended to a journal, and the state of the tournament is rebuilt from that journal.

**The engine proposes, the director decides.** Nothing is ever applied on its own. A warning — an inconsistent score, a match played by the wrong player, a match expected to end during the meal break — is stated, not imposed: the director knows things the engine does not.
What it does not do
It has no interface. It stores nothing. It displays no sentence: everything that leaves the engine is a **code**, which the host software renders in its user's language.
It breaks no ties. Ties stay ties, or are settled by a play-off. No ranking is decided by a hidden criterion.
It has never run a real tournament. It is tested by simulation — thousands of tournaments played on every change — but a simulation is not a playing hall.

The name

Nicomachus was Aristotle's son, and the addressee of the *Nicomachean Ethics*, which asks what makes a decision a just one. Running a tournament consists of making a great many of them, fast, in front of people who are waiting.
deroulement: How a tournament unfolds
This page describes a tournament day from the director's point of view, and what the engine does at each step. Nothing here assumes any knowledge of programming.
Before the start: registration

The director registers the players. A player has a name, possibly a club and a rating (the PR: the lower it is, the better the player). The rating is optional — a player with no rating is not a perfect player, and the engine never treats him as one.
A list can also be imported from a CSV file, from a ticketing service or a spreadsheet, and exported again for the next tournament.
The first pairing
As soon as two players are free, the engine proposes a match: two names, a length in points, and a table number. The director confirms; the players go and sit down.

Tables are not mere numbers. A table can be **unavailable** — broken board, table removed — or **reserved** for the broadcast of the final. The engine skips them, and if no table is free it says so instead of falling silent.
During: the results
The director enters results as they come: the winner, and the score if he knows it. The score is optional; what matters is who won.

Every result frees two players, and the engine immediately proposes new matches. This is **continuous** mode: nobody is kept waiting. It has a known flaw — a player finishing at 2:03 pm could choose his opponent by reporting at 2:04 or at 2:20. **Micro-rounds** close that door: pairings are made in batches, at fixed times, and the engine shows the time left before the next one.
The opposite of continuous mode is **rounds**: everyone plays at the same time, and one waits for the last match before starting again. It is simpler to follow, and much longer.
When things do not go as planned

A player arrives late, after the draw. The engine lists the bye slots still free and installs him there **without redoing the draw**. If there is no slot, he is registered anyway and the engine says where he will enter.
A player has to leave at 6 pm. He can withdraw right away — his matches in progress are lost by forfeit — or withdraw **after his current match**, which then runs to its end.
A player does not show up. That is a forfeit for this match only: he has not left the tournament, and afterwards follows the path of an ordinary loser, the consolation for instance.
A match was started by mistake: it is cancelled, and its slot becomes free again.
A mistake found after the fact
A result was wrong. **The journal is never modified**: a correction is one more event, and the state is recomputed from everything that has been recorded.

If the corrected match was in a bracket, the following matches were played by the wrong people. The engine says so, then **proposes the repair**: cancel the semi-final, cancel the final, then restart the right matches. The director confirms, or does otherwise. Nothing is cancelled on its own.
A tournament already closed can be **reopened**: the final standings are cleared, the correction applied, and the standings recomputed at the next closing.
The meal
Scheduled breaks are declared in advance. A match whose expected end would fall during the break is flagged — but **it remains proposed**. The director knows whether those two will eat afterwards.
The end

The standings can be read at any moment, not only at the end. They place players by what they reached: winner, finalist, knocked out in such a round, knocked out with so many wins. **Ties stay ties**: no hidden tiebreak separates them.

The prize money is spread over those standings. An entry fee, an organisation retention, percentages — a poster announces "50/30/20%" and not amounts, since the pool depends on the number of entries. Each prize is rounded to the unit and the remainder goes to the first place, so that the sum distributed equals exactly the pool after retention. A consolation can have its own prizes, on its own standings.
What gets displayed

The engine produces self-contained pages: a single file, which opens offline from a USB stick on the hall's computer. The wall screen shows the actions to take, the table grid, the matches in progress, the brackets and the standings. The pairing sheet prints on one A4 page, with an empty box per player to write the score by hand.
formats: The formats

A tournament is a sequence of **phases**. Each phase has its format, and the survivors of one enter the next — sometimes with their remaining lives. The available formats are the following; the choice between them is justified by [the study](etude_formats.md).
Swiss with lives

Each player starts with a number of **lives** (two, usually) and loses one on each defeat. Players with the same number of losses are paired, avoiding a rematch with an opponent already met and, if asked for, players from the same club.
This is the reference format: nobody is knocked out on the first match, and everyone plays as much as his results deserve.

It is played **continuously** — as soon as two players are free — or **in rounds** — everyone at the same time. Continuous is markedly shorter: the same number of matches, almost four hours less of hall time in a sixty-four-player tournament.

One important option: **the switch**. The Swiss stops as soon as the sum of remaining lives reaches a power of two — sixteen, for instance — and switches to a sixteen-slot bracket, where players with two lives skip the first round. This is the recommended format: the best quality for the shortest duration.
Brackets
**Single elimination** is what everybody knows: you lose, you are out. It is short, and it is brutal — half the field has played a single match.
Three variants soften it:
the **consolation** collects the losers of the main bracket and gives them a second tournament;
the **last chance** collects the losers of the consolation;
**reconciliation** has the winner of the consolation play the winner of the main bracket — and with **recharge**, the winner of the main bracket must be beaten twice. That is true double elimination.
The **lives bracket** is a bracket where a player arriving with two lives skips the first round. That is how a Swiss switches to a bracket without losing anything of what has been played.
Match lengths may grow towards the end: `15, 13, 11, 9` reads from the last round back to the first — final to fifteen points, semi-finals to thirteen, quarter-finals to eleven, the rest to nine.
GSL blocks
Groups of four players, two lives each: two opening matches, a winners' match, a losers' match, a decider. Two players come out of each group.

It is the format players read most easily — each knows in advance how many matches he will play and against whom — and the easiest to fit into time slots. It is also the longest: one waits for the whole group.
Round robin

Round robin groups: everyone meets everyone, following the Berger table. The top finishers of each group qualify for what follows. A tie is not broken on points: it is settled by a **play-off** with two lives between the players concerned.
Seeding
By default a bracket is drawn **at random**, entirely. That is a choice, not an oversight: it is the current culture of backgammon, and the study shows no need to depart from it.

For the organisers who want it, an option places players by rating following the classic construction — first against sixteenth, second against fifteenth — so that the two best cannot meet before the final. It stays off until asked for.

integration: This page is for whoever writes the software that will use Nicomaque. It fits in one page; the [specification](specification.md) gives the detail.
The engine persists nothing and displays nothing. The host keeps a **journal** — an ordered list of events — and the engine rebuilds the state from it on demand.
Three calls are enough to understand the loop:
`Propose()` — or `ProposeAt(now)` — says what there is to do now;
The journal serialises to JSON. Recovery after a crash is a `Replay`.
The three rules not to forget

**The journal is never modified.** A correction is one more event (`CorrectionEvent`), so is a withdrawal (`PlayerWithdrawnEvent`), so is a cancellation (`CancelEvent`). Nothing is erased, nothing is rewritten.

**Nothing that leaves the engine is meant to be displayed.** Match labels, standings notes, warnings and waiting reasons are structured **codes**. It is the host that renders them, in its user's language. A French rendering is provided for the console and the examples, but a multilingual host ignores it.

**Draws are recorded, not recomputed.** The draw event carries the placement obtained. Replaying a journal therefore never depends on the pairing algorithm, and that algorithm can evolve without breaking an existing journal.

The `render` package produces self-contained pages — a single file, embedded stylesheet, no external resource, no script. It takes a translator (`Labeler`) supplied by the host: the engine's codes and the words of the rendering itself all go through it.
It produces the hall screen, the bracket trees with the drops into the consolation, the table grid, the lives board, the standings, and the printable pairing sheet.
